transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-22
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Evan Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Nina Park (Redwood Solutions), Marta Lopez (Aurora Head of AI), Jon Kim (Aurora CTO), Sara Blake (Eng Manager), Devon Price (Product)

[00:00] Evan Miller: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro from us then we can jump straight into the structured output demo — I'll hand it over to Priya for the walkthrough.
[00:08] Marta Lopez: Thanks, Evan. Quick note, we're really interested in deterministic JSON outputs for downstream systems — our reconciliation pipeline breaks if the schema drifts.
[00:16] Priya Rao: Totally, that's exactly what we'll show. today we'll demo Redwood's JSON mode, schema enforcement, and function/tool calling — we also have a quick live example calling a webhook to your sandbox payments endpoint.
[00:25] Jon Kim: Excellent, latency is a hard constraint — we need 95th percentile < 200ms for our lookup calls, but for batch enrichments we're more flexible.
[00:34] Nina Park: Noted — we'll talk about routing and fallback options as well (hosted vs dedicated capacity) and how autoscaling affects p95.
[00:42] Devon Price: And security — we need to understand key management, audit logs, and where the model execution happens (VPC/on-prem options).
[00:50] Priya Rao: Great. quick agenda slide — 1) short recap of APIs, 2) structured output / JSON mode, 3) function calling & tool demo, 4) guardrails & validation, 5) Q&A and next steps.

[01:30] [DEMO START] Priya Rao: Opening the API console — here is a sample request using JSON mode; we provide a schema for the response with types and required fields. example schema: {id: string, amount_cents: integer, currency: string, status: enum["authorized","captured","failed"], metadata: object}.
[01:48] Sara Blake: How strict is the enforcement? if the model returns an extra field or types mismatch, what happens?
[01:55] Priya Rao: By default Redwood will attempt to coerce simple mismatches and return a structured response with a validation layer that reports errors; you can set enforce_strict=true to reject and fallback to a different model or return an error. We'll show both behaviors.
[02:10] Evan Miller: For engineering, the ability to choose coercion vs strict fail is big — you can keep lenient for experiments then flip strict for production.

[03:00] Priya Rao: Live example — I'll call the Redwood hosted endpoint with a schema for a payment validation response, streaming enabled. Watch the streaming frames: each tokenized chunk is validated and assembled into the final JSON output.
[03:20] [00:03:20] (streaming frames shown)
[03:28] Marta Lopez: I see the JSON came back perfectly formatted. What about hallucinations — can the model invent fields not in schema?
[03:36] Priya Rao: If a field is not in the schema, Redwood by default strips unknown keys during strict mode; there's also a validation report you can inspect that lists unknown fields and confidence scores per field.
[03:48] Jon Kim: Does that validation happen client-side or in the serving runtime? I ask because we have compliance needs to keep logs in our VPC.
[03:56] Nina Park: Validation is done in the service layer tied to your deployment. For Private deployments we can run the entire control plane and validation inside your VPC; logs can be sent to your SIEM via syslog or S3 with encryption.

[05:10] Priya Rao: Next, function/tool calling. We're going to simulate a tool call to Aurora's sandbox webhook that returns account status. We'll show how the model emits a structured call request, Redwood routes it securely, and returns the tool response back into the JSON flow.
[05:30] [DEMO] Priya Rao: Triggering function call -> model responds with {"tool":"payments_lookup","args":{"account_id":"acct_9234"}}; Redwood performs an authenticated POST (we configured a signed webhook) and the tool output is injected into the final structured response.
[05:50] Devon Price: Are credentials stored in Redwood or can we use customer-managed keys?
[05:56] Priya Rao: You can use Redwood-managed secrets, or for Private you can integrate with your KMS/HSM. We also support short-lived credentials and token exchange patterns so Redwood never stores long-lived plaintext keys.

[07:05] Sara Blake: How do you prevent the model from calling arbitrary tools? we don't want accidental calls to production endpoints.
[07:12] Priya Rao: Good question. We lock tool definitions to explicit schemas and whitelisted endpoints per deployment/environment. For hosted flows you get RBAC and scope tokens per tool; for Dedicated/Private you get fine-grained network policies and we honor your allowlists.

[08:00] Priya Rao: Showcasing guardrails — we have rate limits for tool calls, retry/backoff policies, and sandboxing options. here's a rule that denies tool calls if confidence < 0.6 or if the requested resource is in production.
[08:20] Jon Kim: And observability? we need lineage — which prompt produced which call and which tokens were used.
[08:27] Nina Park: Redwood Console provides per-request traces, token-level costs, and a replayable trace you can export. For audit we provide signed logs and an immutable event stream for Dedicated / Private.

[10:00] Priya Rao: Performance note — function calling adds a small orchestration hop. In our benchmarking, simple JSON responses add ~10-30ms for validation, while external tool calls are dominated by the webhook latency. With Dedicated GPUs and local tool adapters inside the same VPC, many customers keep p95 well under 200ms for standard queries.
[10:28] Marta Lopez: We will likely run two patterns: synchronous lookups in user flows (low latency) and async batch enrichment. How do you suggest routing?
[10:36] Evan Miller: We recommend a split: pin low-latency models on Dedicated pools in your primary region for sync calls; route non-critical or heavy context calls to cheaper quantized variants or to off-peak capacity. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization and batching settings.

[12:00] [LIVE POC EXAMPLE] Priya Rao: Now I'll simulate a partial failure — model tries to call the payments_lookup tool but the webhook returns 500. Redwood's policy engine either retries, returns a structured error with code, or falls back to a cached KV result depending on your route policy.
[12:24] [DEMO shows fallback to cache]
[12:32] Devon Price: Nice, so we can define a policy: 2 retries, then return cached last-known-good with a warning flag.
[12:40] Priya Rao: Exactly. You can also set automatic fallback to a smaller local model for degraded scenarios.

[14:00] Sara Blake: On the schema side, can we have nested objects and arrays with required subfields?
[14:06] Priya Rao: Yes, schema supports nested objects, typed arrays, and validations like regex constraints and enumerations. You can also attach per-field confidence thresholds so you can trigger manual review.

[15:30] Marta Lopez: For our reconciliation pipeline, we need deterministic ordering in arrays and stable field names across model upgrades. how do you ensure that?
[15:40] Priya Rao: Redwood's JSON serializer enforces canonical ordering per schema and you can pin model versions. We also provide diffs between versions and evals tied to prompt suites to catch schema drift pre-deploy.

[17:10] Evan Miller: Quick commercial note — for POC we typically provide a 30-day pilot with a small Dedicated capacity plus support from SEs. Would that be interesting?
[17:20] Marta Lopez: Yes, that sounds good. We'll need to align legal and infra teams — Jon will be the infra owner.

[18:00] Jon Kim: On the security doc, specifically KMS integration — we need an architecture diagram showing where keys live and whether Redwood can do envelope encryption with our HSM.
[18:10] Nina Park: We'll include a detailed diagram in the pack — Private deployments support HSM and customer-managed KMS; envelope encryption patterns are supported and we can run a workshop with your security team.

[19:30] Priya Rao: Back to the demo — showing the validation report UI: it highlights fields that failed type checks, unknown keys, and includes token-level confidence. you can export CSVs or integrate alerts to PagerDuty.
[19:50] Sara Blake: Can we auto-create bug tickets when a schema regression is detected?
[19:56] Priya Rao: Yes, Redwood Console has webhooks to push regression alerts; many teams integrate it with Jira or GitHub issues.

[22:00] [TECH DEEP DIVE] Priya Rao: For engineers: the JSON mode is just an additional enforcement layer on top of the generation API. We compile the schema into a runtime validator that executes after each streaming chunk, which allows us to stream and correct partial outputs. This avoids large re-generation loops.
[22:25] Jon Kim: Does streaming validation impact throughput for high TPS use cases?
[22:32] Priya Rao: There's a small CPU overhead per request for validation. In benchmarks, with our optimized C++ validator on Dedicated hosts, throughput drops <5% for typical schemas. We also recommend batching and prefix caching for high TPS.

[25:00] Devon Price: About tool calling — can we host tool adapters inside our VPC to avoid egress?
[25:08] Nina Park: Yes, for Private we can deploy tool adapters inside your VPC; they speak a secure gRPC protocol to Redwood runtime. That keeps sensitive calls within your network.

[27:40] Marta Lopez: What's the escalation path for production incidents?
[27:46] Evan Miller: Enterprise SLAs come with 24/7 support, a named technical account manager, and on-call SE coverage. We'll include that in the commercial doc.

[30:00] [Q&A rapid fire]
[30:05] Sara Blake: Are there lossless logs of the raw prompts and tokens?
[30:10] Nina Park: Yes for Dedicated/Private. Hosted retains minimal logs by default but you can opt-in to full logs with redaction. We provide controls for retention periods per compliance.
[30:30] Jon Kim: Do you have existing customers in payments, any references?
[30:36] Evan Miller: We do — can share references under an NDA. I'll include a short list in the follow-up.

[33:00] Priya Rao: Wrapping up with a quick replay of the function-calling flow — model emits call, Redwood routes to allowed webhook, receives JSON tool payload, validates against response schema, injects into final structured output and emits a validation report.
[33:28] Marta Lopez: Overall this looks promising. main blockers will be legal and our infra gating.

[34:10] Evan Miller: Final recap of next steps: we'll send pricing + SOC2 pack, a detailed architecture/KMS diagram, demo recording, and sample schemas. schedule POC scoping with your infra and security teams for early next week.

[35:00] Devon Price: Can you also include an example of a strict failure mode so our QA can see how errors look?
[35:06] Priya Rao: Yes, we'll include both strict and lenient examples plus the exported validation CSVs.

[37:00] [CROSSTALK — small logistics about calendar invites]
[40:00] Jon Kim: One more question — pricing model for Dedicated: is it flat reserved GPU hours or usage plus reserved?
[40:08] Evan Miller: It's typically reserved capacity (monthly commit) with usage-based overage. For pilots we offer short-term reserved blocks. I'll include an example quote.

[44:00] Sara Blake: Anything we should prepare for the POC?
[44:06] Priya Rao: If you can share a representative prompt set and one sample endpoint for sandbox tool calls, our SEs will load it into the POC and run baseline evals. Also a list of success criteria (latency targets, error rates, schema pass rate).

[46:30] Marta Lopez: We'll aim to send the prompt set and infra contacts by EOD Monday.

[48:00] Evan Miller: Thanks everyone. we'll follow up by Friday with the items we discussed. appreciate the time.
[48:12] Meeting end

[Post-call notes] 
- Recording and demo artifacts to be shared. 
- Customer asked for strict failure samples, SOC2, KMS diagrams, and a pilot quote. 
- Primary contact for POC: Jon Kim (CTO) and Marta Lopez (Head of AI).
